title: How to Run a 1:1 Worth Showing Up For
summary: A good 1:1 belongs to the engineer: their agenda first, a steady rhythm, real topics instead of status, and a written next step. What Grove, GitLab and the research say.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The reminder pops up ten minutes before lunch: "1:1, 30 min." You've got a release to finish, a review waiting and a Slack thread that won't stop blinking. Moving the 1:1 to next week feels harmless. Nothing about it is urgent today. That's exactly why it keeps getting pushed, and why the things it would have caught show up a month later as a resignation letter, or as a project that drifted off course while nobody said a word.

A good 1:1 is one of the cheapest tools a team has, and one of the easiest to waste. When Steven Rogelberg, an organizational psychologist who studies meetings, surveyed 250 direct reports, nearly half rated their 1:1s as suboptimal (Rogelberg, Harvard Business Review, 2022). This post is about the kind that earns its 30 minutes: whose meeting it is, how often to hold it, what to talk about, and how to end it. It's written mostly for leads, with a section at the end for the engineer sitting across the table.

Status already has a home

The most common way a 1:1 dies is by turning into a status report. "What are you working on?" "The payment retry ticket, should be done Thursday." Ten minutes later you've both repeated what the board already says.

Status has plenty of homes: standup, the Jira board, PR descriptions, the project channel. A 1:1 is for the things that don't fit into any of those. A decision that didn't make sense. A teammate who's hard to work with. A feeling of being stuck on the same kind of task for six months. A half-formed worry about the architecture that isn't ready for a design review yet.

If you can answer a question by opening a dashboard, don't spend the 1:1 on it.

It's their meeting

Andy Grove, Intel's former CEO, wrote the line most managers quote about this. In High Output Management, as GitLab's handbook quotes it with light edits, a one-on-one "should be regarded as the report's meeting, with its agenda and tone set by them". The handbook turns that into a rule of thumb: both people add items to a shared agenda, most of them should come from the team member, and if the manager adds more than half, "this is an indication that something is wrong" (GitLab Handbook, 1-1).

Rogelberg's research backs this up. He found that having an agenda strongly predicted how effective a 1:1 was. Both managers and their reports rated the meetings highest when the report helped build the agenda or set it themselves. His suggestion is simple: each person writes a list, and in the meeting you go through the employee's list first, then the manager's, as time allows (Rogelberg, Harvard Business Review, 2022).

Going first matters. When the manager's list goes first, the report's topics end up in the last five minutes, and on a busy day they don't get discussed at all.

A shared doc that works

Keep one running doc per person, shared only between the two of you. GitLab recommends a private doc because performance feedback belongs there. Add topics during the week as they come up, and write each meeting's next steps at the top so the next 1:1 starts by checking them.

Keep the rhythm

How often? Grove's answer was that it depends on the person's experience with the task in front of them, which he called task-relevant maturity. Someone new to the codebase, or new to leading a project, needs more frequent check-ins than someone doing work they've done many times. GitLab's handbook suggests at least once a week, with a minimum of two live 1:1s a month.

Rogelberg describes three workable options: weekly for about 30 minutes, every other week for 45 to 60 minutes, or weekly for some people and every other week for others. Monthly can work for experienced people who can reach you any time, but in his surveys employees rated it the least desirable cadence, and it was associated with smaller gains in engagement.

Whatever you pick, protect it. Rogelberg warns that canceling 1:1s can stall people's progress and make them feel low on your priority list. GitLab calls canceling "a last resort". If you really have to move one, move it, don't drop it, and say why.

The reason is accumulation. One 1:1 rarely changes much. Twelve of them in a row let you notice patterns: the same blocker showing up three weeks running, energy dropping since the reorg, a question about promotion that keeps coming back in different words.

What to talk about

Once status is out of the way, there's room for the conversations that matter. A few kinds come up again and again.

Things that aren't fully formed yet

A 1:1 should be one of the few places where someone can say something before it's polished. "I'm not sure I'm growing here." "I don't get why we changed the API plan." "I think I handled that review badly." If each of those sentences gets treated like a performance verdict, people stop saying them. If they get curiosity, you hear about problems while they're still small.

GitLab's handbook has a useful tactic for this: people often bring up the important thing at the end, so leave room for a closing question like "How can I make your life better?" and don't put it on the agenda in advance. The same handbook suggests the manager aim for about 20% of the talking.

Specific feedback, both directions

"You're doing fine" feels kind and gives the person nothing to repeat. "Your incident write-up last week made the timeline easy to follow. Keep doing that" does. The same goes for concerns. "Be more proactive" is hard to act on. "When the API contract changed last week, I needed you to flag the risk to the mobile team on day one" gives a clear picture.

Ask for feedback on yourself too, and make it easy to answer: "What's one thing I could do to make your week easier?" There's more on how to phrase both sides in How to Give Feedback, and How to Take It.

Career direction, now and then

Day-to-day issues will fill every 1:1 if you let them. Rogelberg suggests weaving in longer-horizon topics like career plans and development now and then. One of his sample questions: "What would you like to be doing in five years?"

When I took technical ownership of a team of 11 after a CTO handover, I started with a 1:1 with each person, alongside watching how the work actually moved. Those conversations turned into a 3, 6 and 12-month growth plan for each person. A plan like that gives every later 1:1 something concrete to check against.

Questions to keep in your pocket

"Is anything slowing you down or blocking you right now?" "What kind of work is stretching you, and what's draining you?" "Is there a decision lately that didn't make sense to you?" "What part of how our team works should we keep, and what should we change?" Pick one or two per meeting, not all of them.

End with a next step

The best 1:1s rarely end with big promises. They end with something small and clear: one decision explained, one worry named, one piece of feedback turned into an action, one next step written down.

Rogelberg's advice is to close by agreeing on takeaways and action items for both people, including how the manager will support them. When both sides write those down, the actions are more likely to happen, and the next meeting has a natural starting point.

Over a few months, those small next steps add up to trust. Engineers stop guessing what their lead thinks. Leads stop guessing what their team is carrying.

If you're the engineer

None of this works if one side shows up empty-handed. If it's your meeting, use it:

  • Keep a running list during the week. Anything that made you go "huh?" belongs on it.
  • Put the hardest topic first. The last five minutes always get eaten.
  • Ask about context you're missing: why a priority changed, how your work connects to the bigger plan.
  • Ask for feedback before review season, so nothing in the review is a surprise.
  • If your 1:1s keep getting canceled, say so. "Can we find a slot that sticks?" is a fair request.

Try this week

  • Open a shared doc for each 1:1 and ask the other person to add the first topics.
  • In your next 1:1, go through their list before yours.
  • Ask one question the Jira board can't answer.
  • End by writing down one next step for each of you.
  • If you've canceled a 1:1 this month, reschedule it today.

The next useful 1:1 doesn't need a big agenda. Sometimes one question is enough: what's getting harder than it should be, and what can we change before it turns into a bigger problem?

faqs.q: Who should own the agenda in a 1:1?
faqs.a: The person being managed. Andy Grove wrote in High Output Management that a one-on-one is the report's meeting, with the agenda and tone set by them. GitLab's handbook adds a rule of thumb: if the manager adds more than half the agenda items, something is wrong. Steven Rogelberg's research found that managers and reports both rated 1:1s highest when the report helped build the agenda.

Weekly for about 30 minutes or every other week for 45 to 60 minutes both work, according to Steven Rogelberg. Monthly was the least desirable option in his surveys. Andy Grove tied frequency to how experienced someone is with their current task, so newer people or new responsibilities call for more frequent meetings. GitLab's handbook suggests at least once a week.

faqs.q: What should you talk about in a 1:1 instead of status updates?
faqs.a: Anything that doesn't fit on the board: decisions that didn't make sense, blockers, friction with other teams, half-formed worries, specific feedback in both directions and, now and then, career direction. Status already lives in standups, tickets and PRs, so a 1:1 spent repeating it is a 1:1 wasted.

faqs.q: Is it OK to cancel a 1:1 when things get busy?
faqs.a: Try not to. Rogelberg warns that canceling can slow people's progress and make them feel low on your priority list, and GitLab's handbook calls canceling a last resort. If you have to move one, reschedule it right away and say why.

With takeaways and action items for both people, including how the manager will help. Rogelberg notes that when both sides write these down, the actions are more likely to happen. Put them at the top of a shared doc so the next 1:1 starts by checking them.
